title: Dynamic priority load-shedding RFC sync
content:
Meeting: Dynamic priority load-shedding RFC sync
Date: 2025-11-03
Facilitator: Aisha Patel
Attendees: Aisha, Marco, Daniel, Priya, Ellen, Sean (SRE), Kara (product)

Purpose: quick sync following RFC draft submission. Align on behavioral guarantees, metrics, and the minimal implementation that unblocks Dedicated and Hosted SLO experiments.

Agenda (30m):
- Recap RFC goals (5m)
- Priority model and token accounting (8m)
- Interaction with batching/KV cache and quantized model variants (8m)
- Autoscaler and rollout plan (5m)
- Action items and owners (4m)

Notes and discussion highlights:
1) Problem statement recap
- Under extreme load (traffic spikes, noisy-evaluation jobs, training-mirror jobs) we need deterministic, explainable behavior to preserve SLOs for high-priority customers and internal-critical flows. Current approach (simple global token bucket + FIFO eviction) is insufficient: it doesn't respect per-customer priority and interacts poorly with prefix KV cache hits (which can spike memory use).
- Goal: implement a dynamic, per-priority load-shedding layer that can preempt/slow low-priority requests, surface clear telemetry, and gracefully degrade (partial responses / fallbacks) rather than opaque failures.

2) Core design (agreed in principle)
- Priority classes: P0 (platform-critical), P1 (paid sla), P2 (best-effort), P3 (batch/cron/backfill).
- Soft token buckets per priority class + a small global reserve for handling bursts across classes. Token refill rates configurable per deployment (hosted vs dedicated).
- When tokens exhausted for a priority, we perform one of: queue with bounded wait (max_wait configurable), partial-response streaming (stream prefix and then close), or preempt/abort depending on route policy.
- Policies bound to route config in the control plane (product will add route-level priority tag). This makes rollback simpler — change route tags to demote flows.

3) Interaction with batching & KV cache
- Important constraint: batching pipeline can hide request counts (one batch with 100 inputs uses same kernel run). We must account for batch-size-adjusted token consumption: treat one batched request as N token usage where N=effective_sample_count.
- KV cache hits: requests that hit KV cache should consume fewer tokens (we discussed weight multipliers: cache_hit_weight=0.2 as starting point). However, cache-hit weighting interacts with eviction heuristics; we will add a metric: tokens_consumed_by_cache_hit to watch regressions.
- Quantized model variants: q8/q4 variants have different per-token latency/cost profiles. The load-shed layer should be model-variant-aware so that low-priority requests can be routed to cheaper quantized variants automatically when available. This requires adding variant tags to the routing decision path.

4) Preemption semantics and graceful degradation
- Preemption order: cancel batchable, long-running low-priority requests first. For single-token interactive sessions, prefer bounded wait + partial streaming rather than hard cancel.
- Partial-response contract: we will add a standard header in responses indicating "degraded: true", and include a short reason code (e.g., "PRIORITY_PREEMPT", "CACHE_FALLBACK"). Product and SDKs will interpret these for UX (Kara to own product mapping).

5) Observability and SLOs
- Required metrics before rollout: per-priority token refill rate, tokens consumed, preempt_count, average wait-time-by-priority, token_penalty_rate (retries after preempt), and failed_streams_by_reason.
- We will add a per-route budget dashboard (console) with heatmap of preempt rates. Traces should include priority tag and token accounting snapshot (so we can debug why a request was preempted).

6) Autoscaling and capacity planning
- Autoscaler will consume aggregated demand = sum(weighted_request_count) where weight = expected_gpu_time(token_count, model_variant). INF-3284 will add a small prediction model for short-term spikes (1-2 min).
- We will keep a conservative safety margin for Dedicated customers in the initial rollout (reserve_capacity_pct=15).

7) Security and fairness concerns
- Risk of priority escalation if route tags are misconfigured. Proposal: require signed route changes for P0/P1 and audit log entries (KMS-backed). Security will review later.
- Fairness: batch-heavy tenants could hide behind single large batch to hog capacity. Mitigation: per-tenant batch-size cap + weight-by-unique-session heuristic.

Open design decisions (requires follow-up):
- Q: exact token weighting formula for cache hits and quantized variants. Priya to prototype two formulas in a small sim. (owner: Priya, due: 2025-11-10)
- Q: How to surface degraded responses in the SDK (error vs metadata). Kara to propose SDK contract (owner: Kara, due: 2025-11-12)
- Q: Backpressure propagation into client libraries vs internal queueing. Decision leaning to prefer server-side bounded queue + client-facing Retry-After header; engineering to prototype. (owner: Marco, due: 2025-11-14)

Implementation plan (MVP scope)
- Phase 0 (spike, 1 week): implement per-priority token buckets, simple preempt logic (abort low-priority), basic metrics. No product-facing partial-response behavior yet. (owner: Daniel)
- Phase 1 (2–3 weeks): integrate batch-aware accounting, cache-hit weighting, model-variant awareness routing. Add metric dashboards. Feature flag rollout in hosted. (owner: Aisha + Priya)
- Phase 2 (2 weeks): partial-response streaming and SDK contract, autoscaler integration, Dedicated conservative rollout. (owner: Marco + Sean)
- Phase 3 (follow-up): circuit-breaker policies, signed route changes, fairness heuristics. (owner: Engineering + Security)

Action items and owners:
- Priya: run weighting sim (cache hit / q4 vs q8) and produce short report with recommended multipliers. due 2025-11-10.
- Daniel: spike implementation of token buckets and preempt logic, initial metrics. due 2025-11-07.
- Marco: prototype client-visible backpressure pattern + Retry-After header behavior and sample SDK changes. due 2025-11-14.
- Kara: SDK/UX contract for degraded responses and mapping to product messaging. due 2025-11-12.
- Sean (SRE): define alert thresholds for preempt_rate and retry storms; add to runbooks. due 2025-11-12.
- Aisha: open minimal PR with config schema changes and test vectors. PR target: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1423. due 2025-11-07.

Risks called out:
- Complexity of accounting across batching and async GPU kernels could lead to wrong prioritization decisions; heavy telemetry will be needed in the first 2 weeks after rollout.
- If partial-response becomes the default, UX for customers may degrade unexpectedly — product needs to prepare fallback messaging.

Decisions made during this sync (finalized):
- Implement per-priority token buckets + small global reserve (agreed).
- Weight cache hits with a starting multiplier of 0.2 and allow tuning via flags (temporary decision, to be validated by Priya's sim).
- Route-level priority tags in control plane (agreed; security to require extra review for P0/P1 changes).

Unresolved and follow-up meeting planned:
- Deep sync on autoscaler prediction model and integrating weighted demand into existing scaler pipeline. (tentative: 2025-11-11, attendees: Marco, Sean, Priya)

Quick notes to self / rough todos in doc body (informal):
- add unit tests for batch accounting: test that 1 batch of 8 with 2 cache hits counts as weight=6.4 (8 * 1 - 2 * (1 - 0.2))? need to formalize formula.
- add flag: enable_priority_shedding=true for canary envs.
- think through metric cardinality: per-route + per-priority is already high; aggregate for console.

End of notes.
Next sync: 2025-11-05 10:00 PT (follow-up on Daniel spike + Priya sim)
